# Remediation patterns (guidance, not a substitute for reading the code)

Verify library names, versions and maintenance status before recommending anything. If unsure whether a PQC
library API exists in the project's dependency versions, say so and propose a skeleton/abstraction instead.

| Finding | Typical remediation | Behavior impact to flag |
|---|---|---|
| SHA-1 / MD5 (CWE-327/328) | Integrity/fingerprint: SHA-256/SHA-512/SHA3-256 (`hashlib`). Passwords: do not use a plain hash; use a salted KDF (scrypt/Argon2id/PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with high iterations). Signatures/HMAC: SHA-256+. | Digest length/value changes: stored digests, DB columns, external comparisons, URLs/filenames break. Offer a versioned/dual-verify migration. |
| CWE-759 "hash without salt" | Only relevant if hashing **passwords/secrets**. Use a salted KDF. For file-integrity hashes it is a false positive: propose `skipped` with that reason. | Password hash format change requires re-hash on next login. |
| RSA / DSA / DH (CWE-327, CWE-326) | Key transport/exchange: ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ideally hybrid with classical during transition. Signatures: ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205). If a PQC library is not yet viable, minimum interim step: larger keys (RSA >= 3072) plus a documented migration TODO, and say this is **not** quantum-safe. | Key/ciphertext/signature sizes grow; protocol, storage and peers must support them. New dependency (e.g. liboqs bindings) needed. |
| ECDSA / ECDH / EC keygen (CWE-327) | ECDH -> ML-KEM (hybrid e.g. X25519+ML-KEM-768 where supported); ECDSA -> ML-DSA. | Same as above; interop with peers. |
| AES with 128-bit key or unspecified size (CWE-327) | Use 256-bit keys (Grover). | Existing ciphertext encrypted with old keys needs decrypt-with-old/re-encrypt path. |
| ECB mode | Use an AEAD mode (AES-GCM) with unique random nonce, or at minimum CBC/CTR with random IV + separate MAC. | Ciphertext format changes (adds nonce/tag); legacy data needs migration. |
| CBC with static/predictable IV (CWE-1204) | Generate a fresh random IV per message (`os.urandom(16)`/`secrets.token_bytes`), store/prepend it; prefer AES-GCM. | Output format changes (IV transported). |
| Weak/low PBKDF2 params | Raise iterations per current OWASP guidance, use SHA-256+. | Stored hashes need parameter storage + re-hash. |
| Hard-coded keys/IVs | Load from environment/secret manager (per project standard: `.env`, not committed); add `.env.example` with `# HashiCorpIgnore` on example secrets. | Deployment config change. |
| Hard-coded password (CWE-259) | Load the credential at runtime from environment or secret manager (per project standard: `.env`, not committed); add `.env.example` with `# HashiCorpIgnore` on example values. Treat the exposed password as compromised: rotate it, since it remains in git history. Never log it. User login passwords are not stored in code or config; store a salted KDF hash instead (see CWE-759 row). | Deployment config change; credential rotation on every system that uses the password; restart required. |
| Outdated cipher: DES, 3DES, RC2, RC4, Blowfish, IDEA, CAST5, SEED (CWE-327) | Replace with AES-256 in an AEAD mode (AES-GCM with a unique random 96-bit nonce per message). 3DES and 64-bit block ciphers (DES, Blowfish) are exposed to birthday attacks (Sweet32); RC4 is prohibited in TLS (RFC 7465); NIST SP 800-131A disallows three-key TDEA for encryption after 2023. Python: do not use PyCryptodome `Crypto.Cipher` DES, DES3, ARC4 or Blowfish, or the `cryptography` ciphers moved to `cryptography.hazmat.decrepit`, except to read legacy data. | Ciphertext and key format change; existing data needs a decrypt-with-old/re-encrypt-with-new path; peers that only support legacy ciphers must be upgraded. |
| Unsafe algorithm and mode combination, e.g. ECB, NoPadding or unauthenticated CBC/CTR (CWE-327) | Use an AEAD mode for all new code: AES-GCM (Java `Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")`; Python `cryptography` `AESGCM`, or PyCryptodome `AES.MODE_GCM` where already in use) or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Treat ECB, NoPadding and unauthenticated CBC, CTR, CFB and OFB as unsafe. For legacy data that must stay in an unauthenticated mode, add Encrypt-then-MAC (HMAC-SHA-256 over IV and ciphertext), verify the tag with a constant-time comparison, and only then decrypt. | Ciphertext format changes (adds nonce and tag); legacy data needs migration; Encrypt-then-MAC changes the stored layout as well. |
| SHA2 or SHA3 with digest below 256 bits, e.g. SHA-224 or SHA3-224 (CWE-327) | Use SHA-256, SHA-512 or SHA3-256 (Java `MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")`; Python `hashlib.sha256` or `hashlib.sha3_256`). Replace SHA-224 and SHA3-224 with the 256-bit or larger variant; never truncate a digest to fit a column, widen the column instead. For keyed integrity use HMAC-SHA-256 (Java `Mac`; Python `hmac`). | Digest length and value change; stored digests, DB columns, signatures and external comparisons break; use a versioned or dual-verify migration as in the SHA-1 / MD5 row. |
| Hard-coded salt (CWE-321) | Generate a fresh random salt per password or record, at least 16 bytes (NIST SP 800-132 requires at least 128 random bits): Java `SecureRandom.nextBytes`, Python `os.urandom(16)` or `secrets.token_bytes(16)`. Store it next to the hash and never reuse a salt across users. A salt does not need to be secret; store it with the hash. | Stored hash format changes (salt must be persisted); existing hashes are re-computed on next login or via a dual-verify migration. |
| Cryptographically weak PRNG for IV, salt, seed or key (CWE-338) | Replace non-cryptographic generators (Python `random`, Java `java.util.Random`, `Math.random()`) with a CSPRNG. Python: `secrets.token_bytes(n)` or `os.urandom(n)`. Java: `new SecureRandom()` for IVs and salts, and `KeyGenerator.init(256, new SecureRandom())` for keys. Do not call `setSeed` before first use; that disables self-seeding. | No format change; keys or salts produced by the weak generator should be rotated or re-hashed. |
| RSA without OAEP: PKCS#1 v1.5 or NoPadding (CWE-780) | Use RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 for both the hash and MGF1. Java: `Cipher.getInstance("RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-256AndMGF1Padding")` initialized with `OAEPParameterSpec("SHA-256", "MGF1", MGF1ParameterSpec.SHA256, PSource.PSpecified.DEFAULT)`, because MGF1 otherwise defaults to SHA-1. Python: `padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)`. This fixes the padding only; RSA remains quantum-vulnerable (see RSA / DSA / DH row). | Ciphertext format changes; peers must support OAEP with the same digest; keep a time-limited decrypt-old path for PKCS#1 v1.5 ciphertexts during migration. |
| Encryption without explicit IV or relying on default IV (CWE-1204) | Pass an explicit IV or nonce for every encryption, drawn from `SecureRandom` (Java) or `os.urandom` (Python). Java: `new IvParameterSpec(iv)` for CBC and `new GCMParameterSpec(128, nonce)` for GCM; read the value back with `cipher.getIV()` or `cipher.getParameters()` when storing. Python: pass a fresh 12-byte `os.urandom(12)` nonce as the first argument of `AESGCM.encrypt`. Do not rely on provider defaults, such as Java `Cipher.init(mode, key)` without parameters or PyCryptodome `AES.new` without `iv` or `nonce`. | Output format changes: the IV or nonce must be stored with the ciphertext and read on decryption; a reused nonce with the same key breaks GCM confidentiality and integrity. |
| Hard-coded seed or source of randomness (CWE-335) | Remove fixed seeds from production code: no `random.seed(<constant>)`, and no `setSeed` or `new SecureRandom(<fixed bytes>)` for keys, IVs or salts. A fixed seed can make output predictable (SHA1PRNG is deterministic after `setSeed` before first use). Use an unseeded `SecureRandom` (Java) or `secrets` (Python). Seeded generators are acceptable only in tests, isolated from production code paths. | No format change; any token, key or salt produced from a fixed seed must be treated as compromised and regenerated; test fixtures may need an explicit seeded helper. |
| Password-based key material without salt or iteration count (CWE-916) | Always derive password-based keys with an explicit salt and iteration count. Java: `new PBEKeySpec(password, salt, iterations, keyLengthInBits)` with `SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA256")` and a random salt of at least 16 bytes. Python: `hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password, salt, iterations)`. Iteration values are covered in the Weak/low PBKDF2 params row. | Derived key values change; data protected with the old parameters must be re-derived; salt and iteration count must be stored with the record. |
| Hard-coded private key (CWE-321) | Never embed PEM or DER private keys in source or resources. Keep them in a keystore: Java PKCS#12 (`KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12")`, password from environment or secret manager) or PKCS#11 / HSM (`KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS11")`). Python: load from a file outside the repository with restricted permissions (`0600`) using `cryptography` `load_pem_private_key`, or from a KMS or HSM. Treat the exposed key as compromised: rotate it and revoke its certificate. | Deployment packaging changes (keystore file and password); key rotation requires re-issuing the certificate and updating peer trust stores. |
| Programmatically editing providers list (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Remove calls to `Security.insertProviderAt`, `Security.addProvider` and `Security.removeProvider` from application code. Set the organization's provider preference order once, in the JVM `java.security` file (`security.provider.N=` entries), delivered with the runtime or through an organization-managed file loaded with `-Djava.security.properties`. Applications then call `getInstance(algorithm)` without overrides. | JVM-wide change: every application on that runtime gets the new provider order; provider precedence decides which implementation serves an algorithm, so test with the deployment JDK. |
| Programmatically editing security properties (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Remove `Security.setProperty(...)` calls, for example for `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms`, from application code. Move the values into the organization's `java.security` file or a centrally managed file loaded with `-Djava.security.properties`. Individual applications must not override them. | JVM-wide change: a wrong value can silently weaken TLS or certificate validation for every application on the runtime; apply under change control and keep the previous file for rollback. |
| Hard-coded provider name (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Use the single-argument overloads (`Cipher.getInstance(transformation)`, `MessageDigest.getInstance(algorithm)`, `Signature.getInstance(algorithm)`) and let the centrally configured provider order decide. Where a specific provider is mandatory (for example an HSM through PKCS#11), take its name from configuration, validated against an allowlist and checked at startup. | Provider selection moves to configuration; a missing provider now fails at runtime, so validate at startup. |
| Hard-coded key length (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Read the key size from configuration (for example `AES_KEY_BITS=256` in `.env`), validate it against the policy minimum (AES 256 per the AES row; RSA 3072 or more), and pass it to `KeyGenerator.init(int)` or `KeyPairGenerator.initialize(int)`. Fail startup when the value is below policy. | Key size becomes a deployment setting; changing it creates keys that peers and stored data may not accept; re-key or re-encrypt data when raising the size. |
| Hard-coded protocol choice (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Read the protocol list from configuration, validated against an allowlist of TLSv1.3 and TLSv1.2. Java: `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` with `SSLParameters.setProtocols(...)` restricted to that list. Python: `ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_CLIENT)` with `minimum_version = ssl.TLSVersion.TLSv1_2`. Never allow `SSLv3`, `TLSv1` or `TLSv1.1`. | Peers that only support TLS 1.0 or 1.1 fail to connect; inventory peers before enforcing the allowlist. |
| Hard-coded algorithm choice (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Centralize algorithm names in one crypto policy class or configuration (for example `HASH_ALGORITHM=SHA-256`), validated against an allowlist, and pass them into `MessageDigest.getInstance`, `Signature.getInstance` or `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance`. Algorithm migration then becomes a configuration change, which eases the move to post-quantum algorithms. | Switching algorithms changes ciphertext, digest or signature formats; coordinate with peers and stored data. |
| Hard-coded algorithm-specific parameters (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Do not hardcode values that define the construction, such as the RSA public exponent passed via `BigInteger.valueOf(...)` to `RSAKeyGenParameterSpec`, curve names or DH group parameters. Put them in configuration with a policy value and validate them at startup. Keep the standard RSA public exponent 65537 as one named constant and reject smaller values. | Changing a parameter breaks interoperability with existing keys and peers; keys generated under the old value stay valid only while the new policy still accepts them. |
| Hard-coded ciphersuite choice (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Do not hardcode the array passed to `setEnabledCipherSuites` (on `SSLSocket` or `SSLEngine`) or `SSLParameters.setCipherSuites`. Rely on JDK defaults, which already exclude anything in `jdk.tls.disabledAlgorithms`, or use an allowlist from configuration limited to AEAD suites with forward secrecy from the approved list in the coding standards (for example `TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384`). Python: take the OpenSSL-format list for `ssl.SSLContext.set_ciphers` from configuration. | Peers without a common suite fail the handshake; validate with a test matrix against each peer and keep the allowlist configurable. |
| Hard-coded certificate (CWE-321) | Move certificates and trust anchors out of code into a truststore, or a file path read from configuration. Java: load a `KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12")` truststore and use it to initialize `TrustManagerFactory.getInstance(TrustManagerFactory.getDefaultAlgorithm())`, or parse a file with `CertificateFactory.getInstance("X.509")`. Python: `ssl.create_default_context(cafile=<path from configuration>)`. Certificates are public, so the goal is maintainability and rotation, not secrecy. | Certificate rotation becomes a truststore or configuration update; the truststore file must be deployed with the application; trust anchor changes affect all peers. |
| Directly setting protocols or ciphersuites on SSL objects (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Remove per-object overrides (`SSLSocket.setEnabledProtocols`, `SSLEngine.setEnabledCipherSuites`, `SSLParameters.setProtocols`) from application code. Build one `SSLContext` from a central policy (see the protocol and ciphersuite rows) and reuse it. Python: set `minimum_version` and `set_ciphers` once, in a single factory function. | Connections that relied on a per-socket override change behavior once the central policy applies; verify with integration tests against each peer. |
| Setting SSL context as system default (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Remove `SSLContext.setDefault(...)` and `HttpsURLConnection.setDefaultSSLSocketFactory(...)`. Create a dedicated `SSLContext` per component (`SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")`, initialized with its key and trust managers and the allowlisted protocols) and pass it explicitly to clients and servers. Python: pass an explicit `ssl.SSLContext` per connection; do not monkey-patch `ssl._create_default_https_context`. | Global change: every library in the process that uses the default context changes behavior; verify all consumers. |
| Hard-coded mode choice (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Do not embed the mode in a transformation literal such as `AES/CBC/PKCS5Padding`. Build the transformation from a configured mode validated against an allowlist (GCM first; CBC only where legacy requires it), and always name mode and padding explicitly: SunJCE falls back to ECB and PKCS5Padding when they are omitted. | Changing the mode changes the ciphertext format and needs data migration; each mode has its own IV or nonce rules (see the explicit IV row). |
| Hard-coded iteration count, PBE and password hashing (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Read the iteration count from configuration with an enforced policy minimum. For PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, current OWASP Password Storage guidance is 600,000 iterations; NIST SP 800-132 recommends at least 1,000 only as a floor, which is the threshold QSE checks. Store the iteration count with each derived value or password hash so it can be raised later without breaking verification. | Higher counts increase derivation and login latency; existing hashes are re-hashed on next successful login when parameters are stored per hash. |
| Hard-coded tag length (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Use the full 128-bit tag: Java `new GCMParameterSpec(128, nonce)`, with the length from one named constant; Python `AESGCM` always appends a 16-byte tag. NIST SP 800-38D allows 128, 120, 112, 104 or 96 bits (64 or 32 only for specific applications); reject tags shorter than the policy minimum on decryption. For MACs keep the full digest length (for example 256 bits for HMAC-SHA-256). | Tag length is part of the ciphertext or MAC format; changing it breaks verification of existing data unless both lengths are accepted during migration. |
| Hard-coded IV length (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Derive the IV length from the cipher instead of a literal: `cipher.getBlockSize()` in Java for CBC and CTR (16 bytes for AES), and 12 bytes for GCM, which NIST SP 800-38D recommends for interoperability. Generate the bytes with `SecureRandom` (Java) or `os.urandom` (Python) and never reuse a nonce with the same key. | IV or nonce length is part of the ciphertext format; changing it breaks decryption of existing data unless both lengths are accepted during migration. |
| Hard-coded salt length, PBE (crypto-agility, no CWE) | Take the salt length from configuration with a policy minimum of 16 bytes (NIST SP 800-132 requires at least 128 random bits). Generate a new salt per key or password with `SecureRandom` (Java) or `os.urandom` (Python) and store it with the derived data. | Salt length is stored per record; changing it requires re-deriving stored keys or re-hashing passwords. |

## Proposal checklist
- Does the fix change any value another component or persisted data depends on? If yes -> BEHAVIOR-CHANGING.
- Is there a compatibility option (read old format, write new; feature flag via `.env`)? Offer it.
- Are tests present? If not, say so and suggest one focused test for the changed function.
- Never implement custom cryptography; use maintained libraries.
